data.title: Excessive Active Directory Object Permissions
data.summary:
Standard domain accounts held permissions over privileged Active Directory
objects that allowed them to reset passwords, modify group membership, and
ultimately obtain administrative control of the domain.
data.description:
Every object in Active Directory carries an access control list defining which
security principals may read and modify it. Rights such as GenericAll,
GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, and ForceChangePassword permit the holder to
take control of the object they are granted over.

Permissions of this type accumulate over time through delegation performed for
operational convenience, through membership of nested groups, and through
application installations that request broad rights. Because they are not
visible in the standard administrative interface without inspecting each object
individually, they routinely remain in place long after the original business
need has ended.

The environment was found to contain permission chains allowing standard accounts
to reach privileged objects through a sequence of such rights. Each individual
step appears to be a legitimate delegation; the risk arises from the chain as a
whole.

Exploitation requires no software vulnerability and no elevated privileges. The
attacker uses the directory exactly as designed, which makes the activity
difficult to distinguish from normal administrative work.
data.impact:
An attacker holding any standard domain account could escalate to full
administrative control of the Active Directory domain by following the permission
chain, without exploiting a software vulnerability and without triggering
controls that monitor for exploitation activity. This grants access to every
domain-joined system and the data it holds.
data.recommendation:
1. Review the access control lists of all privileged objects, including
   administrative groups, service accounts, domain controller computer objects,
   and the domain object itself, and remove rights not required for current
   operations.

2. Map existing permission chains using an attack path analysis tool such as
   BloodHound, and prioritise remediation of the chokepoints through which the
   greatest number of paths pass.

3. Delegate administrative rights through purpose-specific groups scoped to
   organisational units, rather than granting rights directly to individual
   accounts or to broad groups.

4. Implement a tiered administration model so that accounts used to manage
   workstations cannot be used to reach domain controllers.

5. Enable auditing of directory object modification and alert on changes to
   privileged group membership and to access control lists on sensitive objects.

6. Repeat the attack path analysis on a recurring basis, as new permissions are
   introduced continuously through normal operations.
